source: DooM competition metadata (videos.csv) and lab datasheets

text: One mouse follows another and both mice are in constant movement for a trajectory of at least 2 body lengths of the chaser.
The chase ends when the chaser stops.
Not dependent on speed or distance between the chased and chaser.
If the chaser is near the chased mouse, the head of the chaser should be behind the tail of the escaper. Anyway, the chaser should follow the path of the escaper.
A chase that continues through a shelter/elevated area will be divided and won’t be considered as one chase.
If a subject avoids (see definition below) and then is immediately chased, consider it as chase and not avoid.
However, repeated avoids are not a chase if the requirements above don’t hold.
Mutual sniffing in a circular movement is not considered a chase.
A chain of more than 2 animals that chase each other is still a chase.
One mouse bites, attempts to bite, or prominently pushes and kicks another mouse.
Might occur with few consequent episodes with chase/avoid and sniffing or Chase-Attack (see definition below) between them. Each episode is a separate event.
A quick head movement towards a subject with no bite is not considered an attack.
Sniffing before or after the attack is not part of it.
Repelling or holding back an opponent attack is not considered as an attack.
The chaser attacks (see above; e.g., bites or otherwise seems to be trying to inflict physical harm to) the escaper during the chase.
Can occur between attacks.
The Chaser head must be behind the escaper back.

If the subjects stop the chasing movement during the biting phase and/or if the biting phase is extremely aggressive (throwing each other upside down and so on) it will be considered as an attack. If the chases before/after the attack fit the protocol, it can be considered as chases.
One mouse moves at least 2 body-lengths away from another mouse, who is not moving more than half a body-length, at least until the avoiding mouse is at least 2 body-lengths away.
Occurs only after a contact between two subjects (i.e., they are less than 1 body-length apart).
The event starts when the avoiding animal starts moving its head away and ends when the avoider stops moving or enters the nest (half of the body is inside).
Any one of the two mice can be the one who initially approached the other.
Avoid does not have to be in a straight line from the subject.
Do not annotate as ‘avoid’ if it occurs immediately after a chase (see above) or from the nest, i.e., when the other mouse remains in the nest.
A failed attempt to bite/kick/push followed by avoidance is still considered an avoid.
If two mice fight/attack, and a third mouse consequently runs away, it will be considered as avoid from both.
Quickly passing by a mouse who is standing still should not be considered as an avoid from this mouse.
When mouse A is avoiding mouse B and then approaches mouse C, without stopping between the two events (meaning the avoid is still ongoing while it is approaching), both behaviors are annotated.
For brevity, we will call the mouse that is approaching ‘A’ and the mouse that is being approached ‘B’.

Before the event the mice are not in contact (distance of at least one body-length between them). The event starts when A’s head is directed towards B and A starts moving towards B (not necessarily in a straight line).
During the event, A’s whole body must move towards B (not only stretching its body). Thus, the back limbs should move at least a distance of half a body size (~ 3 cm).

The event can end in two ways. Contact: A stops and the distance between the head of A and the head/body/tail of B is less than ~ 3 cm (less than half a body size). Not a contact: B moves away before A reaches B. A must pass through the original location of B. However, when B starts moving, the approach event ends (if A keeps going after B this is a chase, if A stops this is an avoid).
Two mice can approach each other in parallel. Define the appropriate start/end frame for each mouse separately, according to the protocol.

The following events should not be considered as approach: two mice pass each other and none of them show any interest in the other; one mouse passes another static mouse without showing any interest; A approaches B while B is in contact with a third mouse (if A is not showing interest in the third mouse, A approached only B but not the third mouse); if A approaches B while also stretching towards a third mouse C, this does not qualify as A approaching C.
The mouse is on its back legs, exploring his area – the wall, elevated areas or the open area.
When a mouse is "looking up" but its front limbs are on the ground, do not count it as rearing.
When eating, the mouse will probably be in rearing position. Do not count it as rearing.
The front limbs can lean on an elevated surface.
If the front limbs are on another mouse, do not count this as rearing.
Rearing activity could also appear during sniffing when the other mouse is on an elevated surface, but it is different than submissive posture (see definition below).
First frame of an event – the first frame the mouse's front limbs are up (only his back limbs are on the ground). Last frame of the event – the last frame his front limbs are up.
You do not have to see the front limbs on the wall, if you are sure that they are indeed on the wall.
The position of the mouse front legs should be high enough so that the mouse body axis is at least 45 degrees from ground.
Mouse is in a rearing position, but the behavior happens during contact with another mouse in an act of submission and surrender. The forelimbs will usually be stretched out in defense.
In submissive behavior the head of the dominant mouse is facing the submissive mouse, from his side/back or in front of him. The dominant mouse needs to be interested in the submissive one.
When the attacked mouse is vigorously pushing its attacker away, rather than just having the forelimbs statically stretched out, it’s not submissive.
experimental mice initiate the approach toward the stimuli mice
experimental mice chase stimuli mice
experimental mice unilaterally sniff anogenital area of stimuli mice
experimental mice unilaterally sniff body area of stimuli mice
experimental mice and stimuli mice are reciprocally engaged in sniffing
experimental mice escape stimuli mice actively engaged in interaction
the initiation of an attack episode by the C57 resident until its resolution, does not include chasing or other agonistic displays.
Behaviors consisting of mounting, chasing, vigorous grooming (both paws on face or body), tail rattling, circling of intruder, intruder is submissive during these states.
Direct anogenital sniffing, body face sniffing and intruder not submissive.
Resident investigates Intruder with their nose within ~0.5 inch or makes physical contact with their nose on any body area of the Intruder except the anal-genital area.
Resident makes physical contact with their nose on the anal-genital area of Intruder.
Resident quickly approaches Intruder and initiates biting, tumbling, and/or wrestling events.

Resident quickly approaches Intruder from behind and makes quick burst of pelvic thrusting motions. The mount ends when the Resident stops quickly thrusting and walks away or when the mounting transitions into successful intromission.

Intromission begins when the quick pelvic thrusting of the mount transitions into slower consistent pelvic thrusting motions. Intromission ends when the Resident stops pelvic thrusting and walks away or when ejaculation occurs.

Resident makes a strong pelvic thrust forward and keeps their pelvis pushed forward into the Intruder for a sustained short period of time (~3-20 sec). Many times, the Resident will fall to their side but remain mounted onto the Intruder until the Intruder begins to walk away.
close contact to any part of the intruder (white mouse)’s body
a suite of intense actions aiming at biting the intruder (white mouse), including push, lunge, bite, tumbling, and fast locomotion episodes between these movements
Clear physical antagonistic interaction initiated by the Resident.

Start: Resident makes physical antagonistic contact with Intruder. Typically, this is characterized by outstretched Resident forepaw(s) contacting the Intruder, while the Resident has an open mouth to initiate a bite. Can also be characterized by the first frame of a slap or quick bite without the forepaws being outstretched.
Duration: Attacks can include tussling, biting, boxing, and corralling as part of the bout.
End: Resident orients away from Intruder. Typically, this is a slight turning of the head to look in a different direction, followed by a relaxation of the body and moving away from the Intruder.
Intruder mouse is running away from or attempting to get away from Resident mouse.
Start: Intruder turns head and upper body away from Resident, attempting to quickly move away from Resident.
Duration: Intruder can be freely running away, can be dragging biting Resident behind it, or can be “popcorning” trying to jump over the Resident when cornered.
End: Intruder stops trying to move away from resident, or turns to be defensive.
Intruder mouse is fighting back against Resident by pushing or biting. Intruder is not instigating aggression.
Start: Intruder pushes, bites, or otherwise makes defensive physical contact with Resident.
Duration: Intruder continues to fight back against Resident. Intruder is most often facing and looking at Resident. This behavior can occur standing or when Intruder has been pushed to the ground.
End: Intruder stops fighting back, often transitioning into submissive or escape behaviors.
Resident is following in the Intruder’s path as the Intruder moves away from the Resident.

Start: Resident is moving toward Intruder as Intruder moves away. Typically, this is characterized by the Intruder running away after an attack ends and the Resident follows directly after, or when the Intruder walks past the Resident and the Resident markedly changes directions to pursue the Intruder.

Duration: The Intruder is quickly moving away from the Resident, typically in a straight line until it reaches the edge of the area, at which point it will turn to face and watch the Resident. Resident is moving along the same path as the Intruder without sniffing or foraging in the arena.
End: Either mouse stops moving, or the Resident deviates from path of the Intruder.
Can occur between same sex animals. Resident mounts intruder and paw movement and pelvic thrusts may be present.
Start: Resident covers Intruder and tucks pelvis.
Duration: Resident continues to cover Intruder, can show pelvic thrusts but is not biting or otherwise attacking Intruder. Resident can continue trying to move away but Resident does not let go.
End: Resident untucks pelvis, starts to attack Intruder, or moves to the side.
Resident is sniffing the anogenital region of the Intruder. Resident must be sniffing at base of tail, not further up on back or on legs.
Start: Resident mouse is clearly sniffing anogenital region of Intruder, rather than side, back, or leg.
Duration: Uninterrupted sniffing of anogenital region.
End: Resident moves head away from anogenital region, either to move away from Intruder or to sniff non-anogenital region.
When female subject interacts with an intruder using their nose
When male intruder follows the female’s anogenital area and sniffs.
When male intruder attempts to mount the female animal. The front paws of the male intruder will be placed on the female’s back.
When male animal performs an intromission to the female animal and shows pelvic thrusting
When female animal shows self-grooming of their genitals.
When female stands up.
The nose of the animals needs to be around the anogenital region (tail base in the videos) of the other animals within ±1 cm.
